beginner.headline: Some Young People Could Get Less Government Support
beginner.brief: Some people under 25 could get less money from the government under new plans. Benefits are government payments to help people who need support. Alan Milburn's report is expected to suggest changes to benefits for illness or disability. Under the plans, young people would get a basic payment instead. Some could get extra money for daily costs linked to their health problems. People with more serious disabilities who cannot work would get a higher payment. The report is also expected to suggest more help for young people looking for work. This could include work experience and help from personal advisers. Milburn said the changes would affect people already getting benefits and new people asking for them.

intermediate.headline: Young People Could Receive Less Support Under Welfare Proposals
intermediate.brief: A review ordered by the government could lead to some young people receiving less financial support. According to the Times, Alan Milburn's report will recommend moving people under 25 off the main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn has been asked to help reduce the number of young adults who are not in education, employment or training. Under the proposals, young people would receive an allowance at the same standard rate as universal credit. Some could qualify for an additional allowance to cover everyday costs linked to their health conditions. People with more severe disabilities who cannot work would receive a new benefit at a higher rate. The report is also expected to recommend billions in spending on employment support, including work placements and personal advisers. Milburn said the changes would affect both existing claimants and people making new claims. Young people could lose some financial support if they did not take part in the employment support offered. If the recommendations were approved, it could take almost ten years for the government to save money. Milburn said the new system would require significant investment and would need to be built again from the beginning. A government spokesperson promised to keep support available for people who most need protection and those unable to work.

advanced.headline: Milburn Review Could Reshape Welfare Support for Under-25s
advanced.brief: A review commissioned by the government is expected to recommend a radical overhaul that could reduce some young people's welfare entitlements. According to the Times, Alan Milburn's report will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. The government has tasked Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, with helping reduce the proportion of 18- to 24-year-olds outside education, employment or training, reported as one in eight. The report is expected to propose ending under-25s' eligibility for the health element of universal credit and for personal independence payment, both forms of state support. A replacement allowance would match the basic universal credit rate. Some people could receive additional help with everyday expenses associated with their conditions. Those with more serious disabilities who are unable to work would receive a new payment at a higher rate. Milburn is also expected to recommend billions in employment support, including work placements, job subsidies and individual advisers. Milburn frames the central choice as whether to prioritise young people's longer-term life chances or their immediate financial circumstances. He has warned that the changes would involve difficult consequences for both existing and new recipients. The proposed approach would combine incentives with sanctions, since young people could lose some support if they did not engage with the additional employment services. Milburn says substantial spending would be needed to rebuild the system from scratch. Were Milburn's recommendations to be approved, monetary savings for the British state could still take almost a decade to emerge. A government spokesperson has promised a safety net for the most vulnerable and those unable to work. The government is expected to pursue legislation implementing the plans in the new year.
